title: Agents and model groups
text: Agents and model groups An agent defines the instructions, capabilities, and tools for a task. A model group selects the coding tool, authorization, and model that execute it. Agents can bind several groups or inherit defaults. Repository records select independent Git access. See Model groups and agents.

title: Workflows, runs, and human gates
text: Workflows, runs, and human gates A workflow is a graph of steps and transitions. You can start a published version. Each run records its inputs, active nodes, conversations, and artifacts. A human gate pauses the run for a decision, then follows the applicable transition. The run page, inbox, and artifacts help you follow that work.
keywords: FSM agent Solo gate sandbox artifact MCP

title: Solo and sandboxes
text: Solo and sandboxes Solo is a task session where you can continue a conversation. Both Solo and workflows execute in sandboxes managed by the gateway. A sandbox provides a workspace, terminal, and optional IDE and app preview. The gateway selects an image or template. Grasp requests environments for sessions and runs as needed. See Solo sessions and Sandbox lifecycle.

title: Paste into a remote desktop
text: Paste into a remote desktop After taking control of a sandbox Browser or Computer view, select a remote input and press Ctrl+V (⌘V on macOS) to paste up to 128 KiB of plain text from your device. The paste shortcut uses the sandbox clipboard while the screen keeps focus after a copy or cut shortcut updates it, or after you select Copy to sandbox clipboard in the toolbar. Moving focus away gives priority to text from your device again. If your device clipboard has no text, the shortcut tries pasting from the sandbox clipboard. You can also enter text in the toolbar’s Clipboard dialog and select Paste into focused window. To paste into the terminal on a computer sandbox, select Terminal paste (Ctrl+Shift+V) first. You can still paste from your device after pressing Ctrl+C to interrupt a terminal command.

title: Review workspace changes
text: Review workspace changes Open Changes in the toolbar of a Solo session or workflow run to see the branch and line counts for each repository. Select a repository to open its file diffs. The cumulative view compares against the initial checkout and includes changes after the agent commits them. The last archived view remains available after the workflow releases its sandbox. When multiple workspaces are available, use Workspace next to the file counts to switch which files and line totals are shown. Open Turn changes above the composer to see what changed between the start and end of the last turn. Diffs show syntax highlighting and line markers for recognized code files. The viewer offers read-only source and rendered Markdown. For deleted files, it shows the version before deletion.
keywords: FSM agent Solo gate sandbox artifact MCP

title: @ references in Solo
text: @ references in Solo Type @ to search in the Solo composer, including when starting a session from the home page. You can also choose a reference type from the + menu. Your other Solo sessions, searched by title; closed sessions work too. The agent first sees a summary of the user’s requests in that session and reads the full conversation page by page with the grasp-tool read_reference tool. It sees the session as it was when the turn began; later messages there are not included. GitHub issues and pull requests in the repositories mounted in the current session, or the repositories picked on the home page when starting one. You can also type #number or paste an issue or PR link. Grasp checks access with the same Git credential the sandbox uses, and the agent reads the latest text, comments and diff with gh inside the sandbox. GitHub discussions can be searched by keyword or number using a repository credential with read access to discussions. You can also paste a discussion link directly. The agent can read the body, accepted answer, and visible replies from a public page while signed out. For private discussions, each read uses the target repository’s credential and follows separate pages for comments and their replies. Workspace artifacts can be searched by filename. Sending a message pins the file version. Opening the file from the message or using read_reference to read a text excerpt or download the original file retrieves that version. Use ↑ ↓ to choose, Enter to confirm, Tab to switch types, and Esc to close. On a phone, tap Discussion or Artifacts and keep typing to narrow the results. Enter with nothing highlighted sends the message as typed. A message can carry up to 5 references. The selected references appear above the composer. Delete the @title text or click × to remove one. The agent uses referenced content only as source material. Workflows support the same references: In the home page Workflow composer, pick a workflow, then type @ or use the + menu. GitHub search uses the repositories bound to the workflow. You can search sessions and artifacts with or without a repository. A message with only references can start a run, which is then titled after the first reference. Switching workflows or back to Solo clears the picked references and keeps the text. In clarification and review chats and gate hot revisions, GitHub search uses the repositories the run cloned. The current node’s agent uses read_reference for sessions and artifacts. It reads GitHub references in the sandbox and selects the target repository’s credential again when reopening a discussion. References are unavailable when the node is finished, inactive or its composer is locked, and the anonymous shared approval page does not offer them.
keywords: FSM agent Solo gate sandbox artifact MCP

title: Artifacts and tools
text: Artifacts and tools Artifacts are task data read and written by workflow nodes, such as requirements, plans, test reports, and attachments. Downstream steps can reference upstream artifacts. Grasp provides applicable workflow, conversation, and artifact operations through built-in agent tools. Open Settings → Integrations to browse the catalog.

title: Set up a credential and model group
text: Set up a credential and model group In the setup prompt, choose Coding tool authorization or Model API. You can also add an account under Settings → Credentials. For a model API, save the key and endpoint with the provider’s protocol. For tool authorization, sign in or save the credential requested by that tool. Create a model group with a coding tool, the saved credential or API account, and a main model. Use the provider’s exact model ID, including any slash. Select the group for the agents created during setup. You can choose groups per role. One model you can call successfully is enough to check the connection.

title: Prepare a repository
text: Prepare a repository Setup can register one Git repository. For a public repository, enter its URL. For a private repository, save a token or SSH key, select it on the repository record, and check the host, protocol, and commit identity. You can skip the repository for a conversation-only test. See Repositories and Git access. Setup creates the selected role agents, a Solo agent, and a published default workflow. Start a task to verify them.

title: Verify Solo
text: Verify Solo On the home page, choose Solo and an agent that is bound to your model group. Send a short request such as “List the files you can access in this directory and tell me whether a repository was cloned.” When you get a reply, open its run information to check the tool and model. If you selected a repository, use git status in the terminal to confirm the directory and branch. Continue with Solo sessions.

title: Verify a workflow
text: Verify a workflow Open Workflows → Default workflow and choose Run. Enter a request and confirm the repositories and branches. Use a small task with a clear result, such as documenting a README step and checking its links. Review any clarification, review item, or human gate in the inbox. Open the run detail to inspect the outputs and result. Continue with Run and review workflows. For an unavailable model, failed clone, or a sandbox that stays in preparation, check Troubleshooting at the stage that failed.

title: Start the published stack
text: Start the published stack The published stack uses host networking. By default, Grasp and the Docker gateway listen on every host interface, on ports 8080 and 8899 respectively. Before starting the demo, use firewall or security group rules to restrict both ports to local access. Anyone who can reach port 8080 can sign in with the demo administrator account. Open http://localhost:8080 on the host. The local demo login is admin / demo1234. Set up dedicated users and a credential encryption key for a production deployment. Check both services from the host. The gateway pulls the sandbox image when you first create a sandbox. To warm the image beforehand, run ./start.sh pull. Then follow Your first run to set up a model and an agent.

title: Back up app data and attachments
text: Back up app data and attachments Keep the database, app data, gateway state, and original deployment key in one recovery set. This preserves attachment references, sandbox records, and saved credentials together. Location Content .localdata/db The SQLite database and its related files. .localdata/app-data Agent configuration and default attachment storage. Include the custom path if you set GRASP_BLOBS_ROOT. .localdata/gateway Gateway records. Deployment configuration and original GRASP_SECRETS_KEY Restore deployment settings and decrypt existing credentials. Sandbox working files follow their own save and restore policy. Pause writes or take a consistent snapshot when backing up application data. If migrated attachments show blob: errors or return 404, check that the database and attachment directory came from the same backup.

title: Create a session
text: Create a session Choose Solo from the home page. Pick an agent, a model, and any repositories you need, then send your first message. A conversation can start without a repository. For a new installation, create a model group first. A session uses a persistent sandbox workspace. Use the run information and tool activity beside a reply to see what the agent actually used. Open the terminal, browser IDE, or preview from the session to inspect the changes. An app preview requires a running service and a registered preview in the sandbox. The deployment controls how it opens.
keywords: Solo chat terminal IDE preview switch model restore attachments

title: Switch models and tools
text: Switch models and tools The picker lists the agent’s bound model groups and their main and auxiliary models. The main model in the default group is selected initially. The chosen group determines the tool, credential, and reasoning configuration for the turn. A turn in progress finishes with its existing choice. Your new selection applies on the next turn. When changing tools, Grasp keeps the working directory and uncommitted changes and passes its saved conversation context to the new tool. The agent can read earlier history using Grasp tools. Some environment or credential changes prompt you to reopen the session.
keywords: Solo chat terminal IDE preview switch model restore attachments

title: Open a terminal, preview, or IDE
text: Open a terminal, preview, or IDE Use the terminal to run commands and inspect sandbox files and processes. Use the preview after the agent registers an app. Proxy and subdomain availability depend on gateway and preview settings. Use a local IDE after an admin enables the SSH gateway and you add a public key. Follow Connect a local IDE. Drag or paste attachments into the composer. Each file can be up to 50 MiB. Workflow chat and agent tests use the same attachment controls.
keywords: Solo chat terminal IDE preview switch model restore attachments

title: Stop, restore, or close
text: Stop, restore, or close Open the sandbox info in the session header to see the environment and its state. Choose Stop to save the environment and free its slot, then Resume when you are ready. File archives and E2B snapshots preserve different state. See Sandbox lifecycle. Closing a session cleans up its environment and restore points. Commit or export code you want to keep first. When capacity is full, check which sandboxes are stopped and which still occupy slots before restoring a session.
keywords: Solo chat terminal IDE preview switch model restore attachments

Use input nodes for requirements and run parameters, agent nodes for roles and objectives, conditions for test outcomes, and output nodes for deliverables. Add a human gate at a decision that needs review. Decide what reviewers will inspect and what they can approve, then reference upstream inputs or artifacts in node instructions. Workflow variables can be used in supported nodes. Save your changes, validate the canvas, and publish the version you want your team to run.

title: Start a run
page: Build, run, and review a workflow
text: Start a run Choose Run, enter the request, and check which repositories and branches to clone. The selection, order, and branches are fixed for the run at launch. To add a repository, register and bind it in Repository settings. Open run details to inspect each node and its inputs and artifacts. A run can queue while waiting for sandbox capacity. If a node reaches its total time limit, is cancelled, or is taken over, the run shows that reason.

title: Review a human gate
page: Build, run, and review a workflow
text: Review a human gate Open the pending item and inspect its conversation, preview, and artifacts. Use the actions available to submit a decision or continue the conversation so the run can advance or return for changes. Check the recipient and expiry before sharing a temporary approval link. A run remains in the waiting state until someone responds. An eligible E2B sandbox can save and reclaim its resources while the run waits, then resume on response. Docker and Kubernetes environments remain until an explicit stop or cleanup. See Sandbox lifecycle.

title: Verify the outputs
page: Build, run, and review a workflow
text: Verify the outputs Once the run finishes, inspect its output node and artifacts. Check that the test report belongs to this run, then verify the final changes and branch. To change how subsequent runs work, edit, save, and publish a new workflow version.

title: Add an account
page: Configure credentials, model groups, and agents
text: Add an account Open Settings → Credentials and add a tool authorization or API account. Some tools use their own login. Tools with a compatible protocol can also use a model service. The form shows the options for the tool you choose. Field What to enter Effect API account name A name that identifies the service or environment Identifies the account in pickers. API key or token A credential issued by the provider Authenticates upstream requests. API Base URL The provider’s API base Sets the destination for model requests. Protocol and authentication The provider’s supported protocol and way of sending a key Changes tool compatibility and request format. Enter a custom header only when the provider requires it. Model ID The provider’s complete model identifier Selects the model to call. Retry catalog loading or enter the ID manually. Save secrets in the credentials form. Agent profiles keep references to credentials or groups. When an authorization expires, update the existing account so its valid bindings can continue to use it.
keywords: model group inheritance credential API Base URL API key Codex primary auxiliary agent

title: Save a model group
page: Configure credentials, model groups, and agents
text: Save a model group Open Settings → Credentials → Model groups. A model group is a reusable combination of coding tool, account, models, and reasoning settings. Field Effect Model group name Identifies the group in pickers and run information. Models with the same name can be distinguished by group and tool. Coding tool Determines which agent CLI starts in the sandbox. Create another group when changing tools. Model source Chooses a tool authorization or a compatible API account and the connection used for calls. Main model The model used by default. Supported tools can select their own default. Auxiliary models Configure roles exposed by the tool or make additional models available. Roles depend on the coding tool. Reasoning options Set supported parameters for the tool and model. The options follow the selected group.

title: Bind the group to an agent
page: Configure credentials, model groups, and agents
text: Bind the group to an agent Open Settings → Agents, then the agent’s model settings. The shared defaults are pinned at the top of the agent list. Inherit defaults to use the default configuration’s groups and default group. Choose groups to bind a set of groups or all active groups. Select a default when several groups are available. Automated workflow runs use the main model in the default group. Disable or delete a group to make its references unavailable. Pick an available group on the affected agent before running again. After a group is saved, other tabs in the same browser refresh their choices. A selection made in a session applies to the next turn. To verify a turn, open the run information beside the reply for its tool, model, reasoning effort, and usage.

title: Choose where to configure
text: Choose where to configure What you want to change Where When it applies API accounts and tool authorization Settings → Credentials Agents resolve bound credentials at runtime. Follow prompts to reopen affected sessions after updates. Models, coding tools, and reasoning Settings → Credentials → Model groups, then bind the group to an agent Session selections apply on the next turn. Automated runs use the default group. Git repository, clone access, and commit identity Settings → Repositories Credentials are resolved when a sandbox starts or restores. Capacity, idle reclaim, memory, and agent inactivity Settings → General Applies after saving. See General settings for timing by field. Ports, database, users, and gateway connections Grasp YAML or process environment Restart the relevant service after deployment changes. Images, templates, CPU, memory, storage, and networking Gateway YAML for the backend Restart the gateway and verify with a new sandbox. Node instructions, total duration, and human gates Workflow canvas Save and publish for future runs. Grasp uses CONFIG_PATH to select its YAML, defaulting to config.yaml. The gateway uses -config or SBGW_CONFIG. A deployment uses one Grasp configuration and one gateway configuration for the selected backend.
keywords: configuration YAML env .env CONFIG_PATH Compose SBGW_CONFIG production Docker Kubernetes E2B

title: Choose a sandbox backend
text: Choose a sandbox backend Backend Use when Gateway configuration Docker You want a local demo or single-host service Docker image, resource caps, and networking. Sandboxes share host CPU and memory by default. Kubernetes You run sandboxes in an existing cluster Cluster access, namespace, scheduling, storage class, and resources. Defaults per sandbox are 2 CPU, 4096 MiB, and 25 GiB. E2B You use templates and snapshots API address and built template IDs. The actual template determines its resources. Use the current deployment examples for your backend. Docker · Kubernetes · E2B The gateway owns image and template selection. Release Compose maps SANDBOX_IMAGE to the Docker gateway image setting. Grasp-level sandbox.image and GRASP_SANDBOX_IMAGE are retired. Docker and Kubernetes environments stay available until an explicit stop, close, or cancellation. E2B idle reclaim defaults to 360 minutes. See Sandbox lifecycle.
keywords: configuration YAML env .env CONFIG_PATH Compose SBGW_CONFIG production Docker Kubernetes E2B

title: Determine the effective value
text: Determine the effective value Ordinary server options use process environment → YAML → built-in default. Fields available in General settings use process environment → saved value → YAML → default. Environment overrides lock the corresponding fields. Compose reads .env as input. Set the container’s environment or mount a configuration file to pass values to a service. Grasp’s memory override defaults to 0, which follows the gateway or template. Reset a saved memory override to 0 for future sandboxes to follow the gateway.
keywords: configuration YAML env .env CONFIG_PATH Compose SBGW_CONFIG production Docker Kubernetes E2B

title: Tell the time limits apart
text: Tell the time limits apart Setting When it starts and what it controls sandbox.idle_ttl_minutes, default 360 minutes An E2B model turn has ended and the queue is empty. The environment can be saved and reclaimed when this interval elapses. sandbox.chat_idle_timeout_seconds, default 1200 seconds A running turn is producing no output or activity. It detects an unresponsive turn. Canvas node duration, falling back to sandbox.agent_node_hard_cap_hours, default 24 hours Caps total execution time for an agent node. sandbox.sandbox_create_timeout_seconds, default 1200 seconds Waits for the gateway to report sandbox readiness, including cold-start work. Coordinate with the gateway finalize timeout.

title: Credentials, access, and backups

When setting advertised URLs and proxies, check reachability separately from a browser and from a sandbox. To offer GitHub device login, set GRASP_GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and restart. title: Connect Grasp and the gateway
text: Connect Grasp and the gateway Configure the Docker, Kubernetes, or E2B gateway with its example. The gateway owns image, template, and resource selection. Set sandbox.gateway_url in Grasp and provide the matching gateway API key. Verify that gateway /healthz is ready. Select sandbox.gateway_transport. The default direct requires callers to reach the relevant endpoints. gateway sends traffic through the authenticated gateway and suits server-only endpoints. With multiple named connections, new sandboxes use the connection selected by sandbox.default_gateway. Existing sandboxes keep the connection they were created with. See the deployment reference and gateway contract for connection and backend fields.

title: Connect a public-cloud sandbox
text: Connect a public-cloud sandbox Grasp registers execution environments as named gateways. The repository ships E2B, Kubernetes, and Docker drivers. Each gateway deployment runs one driver, and a single Grasp control plane can register multiple gateways. E2B-compatible services. Configure the provider’s e2b.apiURL, e2b.sandboxURL, credentials, and template in the E2B gateway. The template must include the Grasp bootstrap and reach the control plane to fetch its runtime bundle. See the E2B template and deployment guide. Other cloud sandbox APIs. Implement a gateway adapter that maps create, inspect, delete, and endpoint discovery to the provider’s API. The environment must support the Grasp runtime bootstrap and session endpoint. Private networks can use authenticated v2 transport. Check the required capabilities, then validate an actual create, connection, and cleanup. See the minimum gateway contract and data channel protocol.

title: Configure app previews
text: Configure app previews Policy Effect auto, default Public direct endpoints use direct access. Private endpoints or authenticated gateway transport use subdomains when a base URL is set. Without it, the corresponding exposure option is hidden. subdomain Use preview.expose.subdomain.base_url and wildcard DNS to give each preview its own subdomain. none Disable this form of preview exposure. direct Available on named connections that use direct transport. For production subdomains, use HTTPS and a root domain separate from the application. Treat a preview URL as an access credential. CDP and noVNC are proxied by the platform, with the raw ports kept on the service side. For desktop IDE access, see Connect a local IDE.

title: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Enable the SSH gateway, register a public key, and connect from a desktop IDE or terminal. With the built-in SSH gateway enabled, you can open any sandbox (E2B, Docker or Kubernetes) from VS Code, Cursor (Remote-SSH) or a terminal on your own machine. You only need the IDE and the OpenSSH client that ships with your OS. The SSH user name selects the sandbox: sbx-<sandbox id>. The gateway authenticates the public key you registered in Grasp, then logs into the sandbox as root. Keys stay in Grasp and are never written into sandboxes; deleting a key closes every connection that used it.

title: Admins: enable the gateway
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Admins: enable the gateway Setting Environment variable Meaning ssh_gateway.enabled GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_ENABLED true turns it on; off by default ssh_gateway.listen GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_LISTEN Listen address, default :2222 ssh_gateway.public_host GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_HOST Host name users connect to; empty uses the host name the browser opened Grasp with ssh_gateway.public_port GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_PORT Port users connect to; set it when a port mapping or load balancer changes it ssh_gateway.host_key_path GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_HOST_KEY_PATH Gateway host private key, generated on first start ssh_gateway.max_conns / max_conns_per_sandbox Same names in upper case Global / per-sandbox connection limits, default 200 / 10 ssh_gateway.admins_only GRASP_SSH_GATEWAY_ADMINS_ONLY Allow only admin accounts When deploying: Expose the TCP port. The Docker Compose examples use host networking, so open the port in the firewall. A Kubernetes Ingress only carries HTTP; add a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service such as the commented grasp-ssh at the end of sandbox-gateway/deploy/k8s/stack.example.yaml. Networks that only allow port 443 may block it. Persist the host key. Every sandbox is served under this one key, so rebuilt or resumed sandboxes never trigger a “host key changed” warning. Keep it on a persistent volume (the examples use /data) and share it between replicas, or clients will warn after every redeploy. Settings are read at startup; restart the server after changing them.
keywords: SSH Remote-SSH IDE 2222 public key

title: Security notes
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Security notes Access is authorized per account: the owner of a Solo session may enter that session’s sandbox, and admins may enter any sandbox; sandboxes without an owner (workflows, tests) are admin-only. Missing and forbidden sandboxes give the same message. Open connections close within a minute when the session is deleted or reassigned, the key is deleted (immediately) or the account is removed. With admins_only only admins may connect. The gateway terminates and re-opens the SSH connection, so it can see session contents. The platform already holds root on every sandbox, so the trust boundary does not change. Only public-key authentication is accepted. A source address is refused for a while after 20 failed attempts within 5 minutes; connections still authenticating are capped separately (64 in total, 8 per source) and never use the authenticated slots. Remote forwarding (-R), agent forwarding and X11 are not supported. Local forwarding (-L), SFTP and the channels VS Code and Cursor need all work. Restarting the server drops open connections; IDEs reconnect on their own.
keywords: SSH Remote-SSH IDE 2222 public key

title: Users: first connection
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Users: first connection Create a key if you do not have one: ssh-keygen -t ed25519. Open SSH keys from the account menu at the bottom left and paste the contents of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub. ed25519, ECDSA and RSA of at least 2048 bits are supported. In a Solo session, click the info icon at the top right, then open SSH connection to choose a local IDE. The menu lists VS Code, Cursor, CodeBuddy, CodeBuddy China, Trae, Trae China, Antigravity and Codex. The picker shows your last choice after you select one. The browser asks to open the app, and the IDE asks once whether to open the remote folder; accept both. The IDE connects to sbx-12@grasp.example.com:2222 and opens /root/workspace directly, with no ~/.ssh/config change. IDE How it opens VS Code Needs the Remote - SSH extension Cursor Install Cursor’s Remote SSH extension when prompted the first time CodeBuddy / Trae Remote-SSH is built in; the international and China editions are separate apps, each with its own row Antigravity / Codex Open /root/workspace through each app’s Remote-SSH link SSH connection details at the bottom of the menu opens a dialog with the user, host, port, project folder and an SSH command such as ssh -p 2222 sbx-12@grasp.example.com that runs in any terminal. For a short name such as ssh grasp, add the optional snippet from the dialog to ~/.ssh/config: One machine can connect to several sandboxes at once, one window each.
keywords: SSH Remote-SSH IDE 2222 public key

title: Connections and sandbox state
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Connections and sandbox state A paused E2B sandbox wakes when you connect, which can take tens of seconds. VS Code times out after 15 seconds by default; if it fails, raise remote.SSH.connectTimeout to 60. A session you stopped or closed is not woken by SSH. The terminal shows why, for example that the session was stopped manually. Resume it in Grasp first. A local IDE connection pauses the idle countdown. An E2B sandbox keeps running with its memory cache while it has an open local IDE connection. The Auto-pause row shows “Timer paused”, with the connection count below. The timer restarts after the last connection closes. The info panel shows the environment type, the idle countdown and the latest save. It offers Save and stop, Wake, Resume and Keep running. Expand Details to see the last model activity and workspace.
keywords: SSH Remote-SSH IDE 2222 public key

title: Resource use
page: Open sandboxes from a local IDE
text: Resource use VS Code and Cursor run a remote server inside the sandbox that uses about 0.5–1.5 GB of memory (JetBrains about 2–4 GB), which can crowd the Agent on small templates. After a Docker/Kubernetes sandbox stops, ~/.vscode-server and ~/.cursor-server are not in the workspace archive, so the next connection downloads them again.

title: Register a repository
text: Register a repository Save a GitHub or GitLab token or an SSH key in Settings → Credentials. For GitHub and GitLab, choose the official host or a self-hosted domain. For SSH, configure the trusted host too. Add a record in Settings → Repositories. Enter the clone URL and select a credential for its protocol and host. A public repository can be registered without a credential. Enter the default branch and commit identity you need. Bind the repository in workflow settings or choose it when creating a Solo session. Repository field Effect Name Labels the repository in workflow and Solo pickers. URL Determines the clone destination and which credential hosts and protocols are allowed. Default branch Sets the initial branch choice at launch. You can choose another branch before starting a run. Credential Determines the account used for access. Revoking or deleting it can block new starts. Commit name and email Set commit attribution within the repository.

When a sandbox starts or restores, it uses the current credential and commit identity for each registered repository. Agent model settings select the coding tool and model. Repository records select Git access. To check the branch and author in a sandbox terminal, run: For a failed clone, check the clone URL, credential host and protocol, and repository permissions. title: Sign in with GitHub
text: Sign in with GitHub An admin can enable Device Flow on their GitHub OAuth App, provide its Client ID through github.oauth_client_id or GRASP_GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, and restart Grasp. See Deployment configuration. When adding a github.com credential, choose Sign in with GitHub and enter the displayed code on GitHub. The resulting credential is available in the repository picker. Use Sign in again on the credential to refresh the token and keep existing references. For self-hosted GitHub, paste a token. Organizations that restrict OAuth apps may need to approve yours. The scopes are repo, read:org, and workflow. Use a fine-grained token when you want to scope access to a specific repository.

title: Save, reclaim, and restore sandboxes
text: Compare idle reclaim, stop, restore, capacity, and cleanup across the three backends. Settings has one idle timeout and one capacity limit. The idle timeout applies to E2B only and defaults to 6 hours (360 minutes) after the last model turn. Docker and Kubernetes sandboxes are never saved or released for idleness; their processes keep running until Stop, closing the session or cancelling the run. The capacity limit covers every backend and purpose and defaults to 15 sandboxes. The same setting supplies the workflow concurrency limit. Behavior Docker Kubernetes E2B Idle timeout Not reclaimed; the environment and its processes keep running Same Counts once the model turn ended and no request is queued; regular terminal use, background processes, and page access leave the timer alone. A local IDE via the Grasp SSH gateway defers reclaim. Native pause when it expires Stop environment Verify a workspace archive, then remove the container Verify a workspace archive, then remove Deployment, Pods, PVC and exclusive resources Native pause, or independent checkpoint then release for multiple points; no file archive Next use Recreate, restore the newest successful archive, reconnect Same Restore the newest successful snapshot and reconnect Periodic running backup None None None Cancel run or close session Delete its environment and every recovery point Same Delete its guest and recovery points; provider reclaims physical storage File archives cover the workspace, excluding regenerable node_modules, .venv, __pycache__, .cache and .pnpm-store directories. Docker/Kubernetes restore does not preserve process memory or temporary files outside the workspace. E2B preserves memory, but TCP connections and external requests must reconnect. Docker shared bind mounts are not removed. Kubernetes storage-class and CSI reclaim policies determine physical volume deletion.
keywords: reclaim restore E2B snapshot Docker Kubernetes backup solo_backup

title: Waiting for humans and active work
text: Waiting for humans and active work The idle interval and Never auto-reclaim below apply to E2B only. The idle interval starts when a complete model turn ends with no queued request, or when a new environment becomes ready. Generating, thinking, running tools or waiting for tool results never counts as idle, and every new turn restarts the interval. The interval is persisted across platform restarts. Page polling, WebSockets, IDE/preview access and terminal activity do not extend it, so dev servers, downloads or background commands left after a turn are saved and paused with the environment when it expires. The exception is a local IDE connected through the SSH gateway: while one is open the environment is not reclaimed, and the interval restarts when the last connection closes. To keep an environment, right-click the session or run under Running in the sidebar and check Never auto-reclaim. The choice is stored on the session or run and survives restarts, recovery and rebuilds; unchecking it grants a full interval again. It still counts toward the running limit and does not affect manual Stop, Cancel or Close. Docker/Kubernetes environments are never auto-reclaimed, so the menu does not show it for them. A workflow waiting for human input can release its idle E2B environment once its turn has ended, while remaining in the waiting state; Docker/Kubernetes environments stay up while it waits. A reply restores it before continuing. Any active node protects a shared sandbox. Manual Stop uses the same save path and refuses while a turn or queued request remains. Cancel is a separate terminal operation: conversation/workflow history stays, recovery points do not.
keywords: reclaim restore E2B snapshot Docker Kubernetes backup solo_backup

title: E2B idle memory return
text: E2B idle memory return Files an E2B guest has read stay in its page cache, and its free memory fragments, so the host hugepage pool cannot take that memory back and new sandboxes may fail to start. Ten minutes after the last model turn, Grasp flushes writes, drops the guest’s file cache and compacts its memory so free memory returns to the host in whole blocks. While the guest stays idle it checks again every 30 minutes and trims only when the cache exceeds 1 GiB, including environments marked Never auto-reclaim. No data is lost and no process is interrupted; the next build or large project read is slower the first time. Docker/Kubernetes containers share the host kernel and are never trimmed. The existing solo_backup.keep name applies to all sandbox recovery points. It defaults to 1 and accepts larger positive counts. Pruning follows a successful new save. Restore always selects the newest successful point, with no version picker or silent fallback from a corrupt archive. Existing archives are migrated with their object references preserved. E2B uses native pause/connect with keep: 1. Larger counts use official named snapshot APIs, release the source guest after committing the exact checkpoint, and prune older independent checkpoints after the new save succeeds. Restore prefers the original paused guest. Only confirmed absence allows a new provider guest from the checkpoint committed by the latest save; the gateway ID stays stable. Multiple points cost additional storage and save time, without introducing periodic backups while running. Archive or verification failure preserves the original workload. E2B follows the provider’s official pause/snapshot recovery contract; failed saves do not prune prior points. Grasp requires no private upload or process-exit receipt. Provider storage monitoring and GC remain deployment responsibilities, and unsaved state is not guaranteed against host power loss or storage corruption. Failed deletion keeps persistent retry intent. Shared snapshot ancestors, templates and live readers protect referenced layers, so keep: 1 does not mean one physical disk file. Once the VM is confirmed released it stops consuming a running slot, while disk cleanup remains tracked. Upgrade migrates saved per-purpose capacities once using the larger value; an explicit new limit wins. Old purpose-specific timeouts, maximum retention, manual leases, periodic backup intervals and version-selection APIs are removed. Lowering capacity does not evict existing work. Standard E2B requires no private extension or custom Dashboard. Counts above one require the official independent snapshot API and fail explicitly when unavailable. Existing enhanced self-hosted deployments must update their storage-tracking API and migration before the gateway switches to standard calls. Update a single provider node only in a maintenance window without active business work, and validate with isolated test sandboxes.
keywords: reclaim restore E2B snapshot Docker Kubernetes backup solo_backup

title: General settings explained
text: Look up the defaults, scope, effective time, and verification for the fields in General settings. Open Settings → General. Numeric fields display the source of their current value. Environment overrides lock the relevant fields. An administrator can change deployment variables and restart the service.
keywords: General settings capacity idle reclaim memory timeout GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB

title: Sandbox idle reclaim
text: Sandbox idle reclaim Default 360 minutes. Minimum 1 minute. Applies to automatic reclaim for E2B. Time starts after a complete model turn when the queue is empty. Opening the page, preview, or regular terminal leaves the timer as it was. An active local IDE connection through the Grasp SSH gateway defers reclaim. A new interval starts when the last connection closes. Changes apply on future idle checks. Verify the timer and backend in Solo’s sandbox information. An individual session can choose Never auto-reclaim or Keep running, depending on the surface. Release Docker and Kubernetes environments by stopping, closing, or cancelling. YAML: sandbox.idle_ttl_minutes.
keywords: General settings capacity idle reclaim memory timeout GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB

title: Maximum active sandboxes
text: Maximum active sandboxes Default 15. Minimum 1. Shared across all purposes and backends. Creating, running, and releasing sandboxes occupy slots. Reaching the limit restricts new sandboxes and restores, and new workflow runs can queue. This value also supplies the workflow concurrency limit. Check the usage and limit after saving. Lowering the limit allows existing work to continue and holds new requests until there is room. YAML: sandbox.max_sandboxes.
keywords: General settings capacity idle reclaim memory timeout GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB

title: Sandbox memory override
text: Sandbox memory override Default 0, following the gateway or template. A nonzero value of at least 1024 MiB applies to newly created sandboxes. Docker and Kubernetes values must fit their gateway limit. On E2B the value must match the selected template. The agent, builds, and browser share that environment’s memory. Create a new sandbox to verify the resources. Enter 0 to clear the override. YAML: sandbox.sandbox_memory_mb. The GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB environment variable locks the field.
keywords: General settings capacity idle reclaim memory timeout GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB

title: Agent inactivity timeout
text: Agent inactivity timeout Default 20 minutes. UI range 2–120 minutes. With no output, CPU activity, or disk activity for this interval, the system first attempts to resume. If the agent remains inactive, it ends that turn. A change applies starting on the next turn. Check the run details for a turn that ended because of inactivity. Canvas node duration and sandbox readiness are separate limits. YAML sandbox.chat_idle_timeout_seconds and environment variable GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC use seconds.
keywords: General settings capacity idle reclaim memory timeout GRASP_CHAT_IDLE_SEC GRASP_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB

title: Identify the failing stage
text: Identify the failing stage Open the run detail, inbox, or Solo sandbox information. Note the failing stage, original error, agent and model group, gateway backend, and whether the environment is new. Keep relevant log context and redact credentials. Start with the first failure. Symptom Check first Next step Unavailable model group, empty model list, or API 401 Credential validity, endpoint, protocol, and agent binding Refresh the account or pick another available group. Verify with a short turn. Model groups Clone 401, 403, or missing branch URL, host, protocol, and repository access Check the saved credential, then retry with an accessible branch. Git access Sandbox remains in preparation Image pulls, templates, bootstrap logs, and gateway health Check the first bootstrap error and then the readiness timeout and template resources. Gateway Capacity error or a queued run Live usage, limit, and environments still releasing Stop unused sessions or adjust capacity. Docker and Kubernetes retain slots until an explicit release. Capacity Preview unavailable Listening app, preview registration, and transport policy Check the service from a terminal, then the exposure policy. Preview settings Saved setting seems ineffective Source, lock state, and whether it applies at boot or runtime Check precedence and verify with a new environment if appropriate. Precedence Attachments missing after migration Database and attachment storage backup versions Restore the same recovery set and verify any custom blob path. Backups

title: A turn stalls or ends
text: A turn stalls or ends Check whether it is waiting for a sandbox, detecting agent inactivity, hitting the node’s total limit, or waiting for a human. Use the run state and reason to choose the next action. Output and CPU or I/O activity affect agent inactivity detection. If a turn has ended, save needed logs and artifacts, then retry a minimal step in an available environment. See Time limits.

title: Understand reclaim and restore
text: Understand reclaim and restore E2B can reclaim an idle environment and restore it on next use. Check whether the environment is stopped, saving, or restoring. To keep a development server running, check the keep-running setting and local IDE connection. Docker and Kubernetes behavior is listed in the lifecycle comparison.
